items.value: Because the speed of light is a constant, a light-year is a fixed, well-defined distance
items.reasoning: A light-year is defined as the distance light travels in one year, so it is a usable unit of length only because the speed of light in vacuum is an invariant constant (about 3 x 10^8 m/s). If c varied, the same 'light-year' would stand for different distances at different times and places, and the unit would be meaningless. A is false and irrelevant (stellar distances do change). B is irrelevant to a unit of length. C is both false in general (light is bent by gravity) and beside the point, since the definition depends on the light's speed, not the shape of its path.

items.value: Both are true: Indian Parliament's legislative power is limited, and constitutionality of an amendment goes to a Constitution Bench
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the British Parliament is sovereign and no court may invalidate its Acts, whereas Indian Parliament legislates within a written Constitution and is limited by the federal distribution of powers, Part III, and judicial review. Statement 2 reflects Article 145(3), which requires a bench of at least five judges (a Constitution Bench) to decide any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, which is the route every challenge to an amendment Act has taken from Kesavananda Bharati onwards. The judgement call is that Article 145(3) is conditional rather than automatic, so statement 2 is worded more absolutely than the Article, but as a description of how India differs from Britain it stands.

items.value: Both statements about the Union Government's administrative-reform machinery are correct
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar's 1950 Report on the Reorganisation of the Machinery of Government recommended that a Minister and a Secretary be earmarked exclusively for pursuing and promoting administrative reform. Statement 2 is correct: acting on the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), the Department of Personnel was created in August 1970 within the Cabinet Secretariat and therefore under the Prime Minister's charge; it later became the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, still held by the Prime Minister. The residual doubt is only over the precise wording attributed to the 1950 report, which is why this is not marked HIGH.

items.value: Article 21
items.reasoning: In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) a nine-judge Bench held unanimously that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected intrinsically as part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. Article 15 deals with non-discrimination, Article 19 with the six freedoms, and Article 29 with protection of the interests of minorities, none of which is the anchoring provision the Court identified.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — Devi Lal contested three Lok Sabha seats in 1991
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: Section 33(7) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, inserted by the 1996 amendment, caps a candidate at two constituencies in the same election, so contesting from three is barred by law. Statement 2 is correct and is the very case that prompted that cap — Devi Lal contested from Sikar, Rohtak and Ferozepur in the 1991 Lok Sabha election. Statement 3 is wrong: the Election Commission has only proposed that the candidate (not the party) meet the cost of the consequential bye-election; no such rule exists today.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 — reclaiming public space and participation, and non-denial of services to unauthorised colonies
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: 'Right to the City' is a concept advanced by Lefebvre and taken up by urban movements and the New Urban Agenda; it is not a codified, agreed human right and UN-Habitat runs no country-by-country monitoring of commitments under it. Statement 2 is the core of the idea — the right of every inhabitant to appropriate and reclaim urban public space and to participate in decisions about the city. Statement 3 follows from the inclusive reading of the concept, under which all inhabitants including those in informal or unauthorised settlements are entitled to basic public services regardless of tenure status. Note that on a strict reading only statement 2 is unambiguously right, but 'the 2 only' combination is not offered, and of the two remaining candidates statement 3 is far more defensible than statement 1.

items.value: Only statement 2 — police need court approval to interrogate an accused in judicial custody
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong on the crucial detail: in judicial custody the accused is committed to the magistrate's custody and lodged in JAIL (judicial lock-up), not in a police station; it is police custody in which the accused is kept at the police station. Statement 2 is correct: once an accused is in judicial custody the investigating officer cannot interrogate him at will and must obtain the court's permission to do so.

items.value: Only statement 2 — parole is not a right, but State Governments do have their own parole rules
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: parole is a discretionary concession and not an enforceable right, and the Model Prison Manual expressly says it may be refused even where the prisoner makes out a sufficient case if the competent authority is satisfied that his release would not be in the interest of society. Statement 2 is correct: prisons are a State subject (Entry 4, State List), so each State frames its own Prisoners Release on Parole rules, such as the Delhi Prison Rules or the Punjab Good Conduct Prisoners' Probational Release Act.

items.value: Ministry of Tribal Affairs
items.reasoning: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 is administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, which is the nodal agency at the national level for its implementation and for issuing guidelines to States. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change administers forest and wildlife law and is a frequent distractor here, but it does not administer the Forest Rights Act; the Ministry of Panchayati Raj administers PESA, and Rural Development has no role.

items.value: Article 14
items.reasoning: A law that hands the executive unguided and uncontrolled discretion permits arbitrary and unequal application, and arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality — the doctrine settled in E. P. Royappa and Maneka Gandhi, under which Article 14 strikes down conferral of naked, unchannelled discretionary power. Article 28 concerns religious instruction in State-funded institutions, Article 32 is the remedy for enforcing rights rather than a substantive guarantee, and Article 44 is a non-justiciable Directive Principle on a uniform civil code.

items.value: The Union Legislature contains elected representatives of the constituent units (Rajya Sabha)
items.reasoning: The defining federal feature is that the constituent units are represented as units in the federal legislature — in India the Rajya Sabha, whose members are elected by the elected members of the State legislative assemblies, mirroring the US Senate and the German Bundesrat. An independent judiciary (option A) supports federalism by providing an umpire for Centre-State disputes, but it exists equally in unitary states such as the United Kingdom and so does not by itself indicate a federal character. Option C describes a political convention, not a constitutional feature, and option D concerns rights enforcement, which is unrelated to the federal-unitary axis.

items.value: A community of persons, a definite territory, independence of external control, and an organised government
items.reasoning: The standard definition of a State requires exactly four elements — population, definite territory, government, and sovereignty — and option A is the only one that names all four, with 'independent of external control' supplying sovereignty. Option B omits sovereignty and drifts into the purposes of the State rather than its definition. Option C describes a nation (shared culture and tradition) rather than a State and again omits sovereignty. Option D describes the internal architecture of a particular kind of government and likewise leaves out independence from external control.

items.value: Both — a retired SC judge can be recalled under Article 128, and a High Court can review its own judgement
items.reasoning: Statement 1 tracks Article 128: the Chief Justice of India may, with the previous consent of the President, request a person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court. Statement 2 is correct in substance: while Article 137 expressly confers review power on the Supreme Court, a High Court is a court of record under Article 215 and has been held to possess the power to review its own judgements, reinforced by Section 114 and Order XLVII of the Civil Procedure Code. The judgement calls are that Article 128 also needs the retired judge's own consent, which statement 1 omits, and that a High Court's review power in criminal matters is constrained by Section 362 CrPC — hence MED rather than HIGH.

items.value: Only statement 1 — India has single citizenship and a single domicile
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: unlike the United States, India confers only one citizenship, that of the Union, and the Supreme Court has held there is only one domicile, the domicile of India, with no separate State domicile. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 58 requires the President merely to be a citizen of India, not a citizen by birth, so a naturalised or registered citizen is eligible — the 'natural-born' requirement belongs to the US Constitution. Statement 3 is wrong: Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 allows deprivation of citizenship acquired by registration or naturalisation on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or imprisonment within five years.

items.value: Separation of powers
items.reasoning: The classical safeguard of liberty, following Montesquieu, is the separation of powers with its accompanying checks and balances, which prevents any single organ from accumulating the power to act arbitrarily. A 'committed judiciary' is the opposite of a safeguard, since a judiciary committed to the ruling ideology cannot restrain it. Centralisation of powers is precisely the condition liberty is safeguarded against, and an elected government, while necessary, can itself be majoritarian and oppressive without institutional restraints.

items.value: the Directive Principles of State Policy
items.reasoning: Article 39(c), a Directive Principle, requires the State to direct its policy towards ensuring that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; Article 39(b) is its companion on distribution of material resources. Concentration of wealth therefore offends the Directive Principles rather than the Right to Equality or the Right to Freedom, neither of which addresses economic distribution.

items.value: A legal (constitutional) right available to any person, not only citizens
items.reasoning: The 44th Constitutional Amendment, 1978 deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, removing property from the list of Fundamental Rights, and inserted Article 300A in Part XII: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' The wording is 'no person', not 'no citizen', so the right is available to non-citizens as well, which rules out options A and C; and since it is expressly retained in the Constitution as a legal right, option D is also wrong.

items.value: A Sovereign Democratic Republic
items.reasoning: As adopted, the Preamble described India as a 'SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC'. The words 'SOCIALIST' and 'SECULAR' were inserted only by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, so they formed no part of India's constitutional status on 26 January 1950. Option A drops sovereignty, which was present from the start, and options C and D read the 1976 additions back into 1950.

items.value: A government limited by the terms of the Constitution
items.reasoning: Constitutional government, or constitutionalism, means limited government: the rulers derive their authority from the Constitution and are bound by the restraints it imposes, so power is exercised within legal limits rather than arbitrarily. It is not defined by federalism (option A), nor by whether the Head of State is nominal (option B) or wields real power (option C) — a constitutional government can be unitary or federal, parliamentary or presidential; what makes it constitutional is the limitation.

items.value: tribal languages
items.reasoning: All three are tribal languages of central and eastern India: Halbi is an Indo-Aryan language of the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh, Ho is an Austroasiatic (Munda) language spoken chiefly in Jharkhand and Odisha, and Kui is a Dravidian language of the Kondh people of Odisha. That they belong to three different language families, yet are all spoken by tribal communities, is exactly the pattern the question is testing.

items.value: All three statements are not correct
items.reasoning: Note the question asks which statements are NOT correct. Statement 1 is not correct: in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) the Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and the Padma Awards are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18(1) and so are constitutionally valid, though they may not be used as prefixes or suffixes to a recipient's name. Statement 2 is not correct: the Padma Awards, instituted in 1954, were suspended twice — from 1977 to 1980, and again from 1992 to 1995 pending litigation — not once. Statement 3 is not correct: the ceiling on Bharat Ratna awards is three in a particular year, not five.

items.value: Statement 1 is wrong on the recognising agency (FAO, not UNCDF); Statement 2 is correct
items.reasoning: Hyderabad was indeed named a 2020 Tree City of the World, but the programme is run jointly by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the Arbor Day Foundation — not by the UN Capital Development Fund, which finances development in least-developed countries and has nothing to do with urban forestry. Statement 1 therefore fails on the agency it names. Statement 2 is correct: Tree Cities of the World recognition is conferred for one year at a time against five core standards of commitment to growing and maintaining urban forests, and must be renewed annually.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 — Tiger Woods was the first winner and Roger Federer has won it most often
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: at the inaugural Laureus World Sports Awards in 2000, the World Sportsman of the Year went to the American golfer Tiger Woods. Statement 3 is correct: Roger Federer has won the World Sportsman of the Year more times than anyone else, taking it in 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008 and 2018. Statement 2 is wrong: tennis players dominate the roll of honour — Federer, Djokovic and Nadal between them account for the largest share — whereas Formula One drivers (Schumacher, Vettel, Hamilton) have won it far fewer times.

items.value: Only statement 2 — the five new sports were included; the motto was not 'A New World'
items.reasoning: The 32nd Summer Olympics were the Games of the XXXII Olympiad, Tokyo 2020, held in 2021. Statement 1 is wrong: the official motto adopted for these Games was 'United by Emotion'. Statement 2 is correct: Tokyo 2020 added five sports to the programme — baseball/softball, karate, skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing — of which skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing made their Olympic debut.

items.value: Neither — finalists were decided by percentage of points won, and England actually won more matches than New Zealand
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: after COVID-19 disrupted the 2019-21 cycle and left teams having played very unequal numbers of series, the ICC ranked sides by the PERCENTAGE of available points won, not by the raw number of matches won, and it was on that percentage that India and New Zealand reached the final. Statement 2 is wrong twice over: New Zealand finished ahead of England on points percentage, and in absolute terms England won more Test matches in the cycle than New Zealand did, since England played roughly twice as many matches.
